meta.title: Who really said "You make a living by what you get, you make a life by what you give"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Churchill — a search of the 2.5-million-word Churchill database returns nothing, and the International Churchill Society lists it as falsely attributed. The real author is genuinely unknown; the usual answer, Norman MacEwan, is itself uncorroborated.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You make a living by what you get, you make a life by what you give'?
meta.ogDescription: Definitely not Churchill. The commonly given alternative — Norman MacEwan — has never been traced to a book, date or page either. Honest answer: nobody knows.

answer.label: Not Churchill — and the real author is genuinely unknown
answer.sourceLine: The International Churchill Society lists it among quotes falsely attributed to him, noting that a search of its database of some 2.5 million words of Churchill’s returns nothing. The name usually offered instead — Norman MacEwan — is no better established: it circulates only through quotation aggregators, with no book, date or page ever cited. We can tell you confidently who did not say it. We cannot yet tell you who did.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Happiness is not so much in having as sharing. We make a living by what we get, but we make a life by what we give.
trail: The negative is solid. The International Churchill Society — which maintains the largest searchable body of his words in existence — puts it plainly on its falsely-attributed page: a nice quote, but definitely not Churchill ICS ↗.

The positive is not. Air Vice-Marshal Sir Norman MacEwan (1881–1953) is routinely named as the author of the longer version above, but we could find no primary source: no title, no year, no page. Quote Investigator has no entry. We publish the name only as a lead the aggregator claim ↗.

We could not date any pre-internet printing of the saying in either form — an unusual and honest blank. Its modern reach owes a good deal to a 2005 television advertisement that used it, which is an amplifier rather than an origin.
source.excerptNote: The fuller form in which the saying usually appears when it is not credited to Churchill. Treat this text as an attributed variant, not a sourced quotation — we have not seen it in any book, and neither has anyone else who has looked.

source.rightsNote: Rights are indeterminate, because authorship has never been fixed. It is not Churchill’s, so his estate’s term to 2035 does not apply. If Norman MacEwan really wrote it, he died in 1953 and the text would have entered the public domain in the UK in 2024 — but that attribution is unverified, so the conclusion cannot be relied on. A short quotation with attribution is low-risk; systematic or commercial reuse cannot be cleared until someone establishes who actually wrote it. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British statesman, historian and Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill is the English language’s default author for any sentence that sounds both weighty and quotable, which is why the International Churchill Society runs a standing page of things he never said. This one is a poor fit even on style: the balanced, uplifting cadence belongs to the inspirational-poster tradition, not to a writer whose actual manner was concrete, combative and considerably drier.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is the honest shape of many attribution questions: the debunk is firm and the replacement is not. We would rather say ‘unknown’ than hand you a second unsourced name to repeat.

items.why: Absent from a searchable database of roughly 2.5 million words of his writing and speech, and listed by the International Churchill Society among the falsely attributed ICS ↗.
Widely repeated, never cited. No book, no year, no page has ever been produced. We name him only so you know where the claim comes from, not because it is established.
Circulates in the form ‘From what we get, we can make a living…’ and is likewise offered without any source.

A corporate television advertisement used the line in 2005, which put it in front of a very large audience. Advertising is a superb distribution channel for a quotation and a terrible one for a citation.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Churchill — that much is settled. The real author is unknown, and the Norman MacEwan attribution usually offered in his place has never been traced to a source the ICS list ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is built on a single clean antithesis — get against give, living against life — and that symmetry is what makes it so easy to remember and so hard to source. Sayings shaped like proverbs tend to lose their authors early.
It is also exactly the kind of sentiment that benefits from a famous name. Said by nobody in particular it is a pleasant thought; said by a wartime prime minister it acquires gravity it never earned.
context.detailsSummary: What we could and could not establish
detailsBody: Established: it is not Churchill’s, on the authority of the largest searchable archive of his words.
Not established: any first printing, in any decade, in either wording.
Not established: the Norman MacEwan attribution — no book, date or page has ever been cited.
Known: a 2005 television advertisement gave the line an enormous audience.
Consequence: because authorship is unfixed, so are the rights — nobody can clear it for commercial reuse.
context.pull: The debunk is firm. The replacement is not — so we say unknown.
